newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. pushes NATO summit, charter with Russia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pushes NATO summit, charter with Russia.

text.p: Leaders of NATO should approve a charter defining the alliance's ties with Russia at a summit next year to decide on the admission of new members, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said Friday.
Christopher made the first formal offer of a charter with Russia and endorsed proposals for a NATO summit next year after talks with German, French and British leaders.
But U.S. officials acknowledged that some NATO members still believed his timetable was too tight.

In a speech outlining the U.S. vision of a "new Atlantic community," Christopher also said talks should begin with other potential NATO candidates after the first new members were chosen and he proposed ways to strengthen NATO's "partnership for peace" program.

He received a standing ovation after delivering, in the same city and theater, an address on the 50th anniversary of a speech by then-Secretary of State James Byrnes after World War II that was a turning point in U.S.-German relations.
Byrnes made clear the United States, which isolated itself after World War I, would stay engaged in Europe and firmly back the restoration of German political and economic unity.
Christopher said such principles "shape our approach to Europe this very day."
Stuttgart Mayor Manfred Rommel thanked the United States, saying it was "exceptional ... that a victorious nation should give so much help, hope and encouragement to the defeated."

Christopher said the "new Atlantic Community" should extend across Europe "transcending the artificial boundaries of Cold War Europe (and giving) North America a deeper partnership with a broader, more integrated Europe."

U.S. officials said a meeting of NATO foreign ministers in Brussels in December to discuss the alliance's expansion eastward, internal reforms and ties to Russia would not take decisions but only set the stage for a NATO summit in 1997.

Christopher said NATO embraced a comprehensive strategy for European security in January 1994 and President Clinton now believed another summit is needed to "complete the implementation of this strategy."
Hence, "I expect our leaders will meet in the spring or early summer of 1997 (and) we should invite several partners to begin accession negotiations," he said.
The Czech republic, Hungary and Poland are likely to top the list of candidates when NATO considers prospective new members.
Officials had been saying for months a NATO summit will be held early in 1997. The possible delay until summer apparently is to give more time to negotiations with Russia.

Although Moscow has long opposed NATO plans to take in new members from ex-Warsaw Pact states, U.S. officials said that since its elections in June Moscow had been intensely engaged in talks with the alliance on a long-term Russia-NATO relationship.
"NATO's cooperation with Russia should be expressed in a formal charter," Christopher said. Officials said the document would set out "rules of the road" for cooperation in Europe.

U.S. officials said the summit would mark the culmination of NATO's efforts to transform itself to meet post-Cold War challenges, including full integration of France and Spain into the alliance's military wing.

Christopher said NATO's partnership for peace program of cooperation with Russia and other ex-communist states should involve non-NATO members in planning as well as execution of NATO missions in a new Atlantic Partnership Council.
He also stressed a need for greater economic integration and swift European Union expansion. He said Cold War divisions were fading but there was still an East-West "economic gulf."
